newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Eastern Europeans welcome Clinton pledge on NATO.
newsitem.headline: Eastern Europeans welcome Clinton pledge on NATO.

text.p: East European candidates to join NATO on Friday welcomed U.S. President Bill Clinton's summit pledge that the alliance would expand as planned, but warned they did not want to be "second class" members.
Clinton said at news conference after meeting with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Helsinki that expansion of NATO would go ahead on schedule at an alliance summit in Madrid in July.

But a joint statement issued after a meeting between foreign ministers from leading would-be members the Czech Republic and Poland warned negotiations with a third country must not water down the rights of new members.

"We trust that requirements for countries aspiring to alliance membership will result from direct accession negotiations and will not become part of any formal alliance obligations toward third countries, in order to avoid any second class membership," it said.

Gabor Szentivanyi, Hungarian foreign ministry spokesman, added: "NATO expansion is a sovereign decision of member states and those wishing to join." Hungary is also widely tipped to be invited to join NATO after the Madrid meeting.
Clinton said all members, new or old, would have the same footing in the alliance.

Russia bitterly opposes the expansion of the former Soviet Union's old Cold War foe to territory once under the sway of the Moscow-dominated Warsaw Pact. Yeltsin reiterated his country's view that expansion was a mistake.
East Europeans, conscious of Moscow's concerns, have stressed the political rather than military aspects of membership.
However, some officials have also acknowledged that NATO expansion is a chance to anchor the region to the West after half a century of Soviet domination.

"(We) hail a democratic dialogue between presidents of Russia and U.S., which is in the interest of development and progress of the old continent (Europe) and of the world," the Slovenian foreign ministry said.

Slovenia is seen as only an outside contender for admission in the first round of expansion, though its officials added they were still hopeful of ensuring its security interests as a full member of NATO as soon as possible.

Romanian Foreign Minister Adrian Severin told Romanian television any treaty between NATO and Russia "could include whether or not to deploy nuclear weapons on new members' territory. This counterbalances the Russian 'nyet' in principle".
Severin acknowledged that Romania's bid for membership lagged behind the favourites. "Even if we run at top speed, the other candidates are a few laps ahead of us," he said.

Analysts said Moscow was trying to gain as many concessions as possible from the United States in the process of NATO expansion, and perhaps to forestall a further widening of the alliance, especially to former Soviet Republics.

"Behind closed doors, I think the Baltics and former Soviet Republics may be a bigger issue than the first round because the Russians know they cannot stop the first wave," said Jiri Pehe of the Open Media Research Institute in Prague.
"The question on the first wave is only how many countries, but I don't think the Russians can now even influence this."

Carlo Maria Santoro, a former undersecretary at the Italian defence ministry and professor of international relations, said in Rome the summit had been "the sort of meeting at which everyone knew what the outcome would be in advance".

"The real question is whether we allow the Russians to continue to have some sort of area of territorial influence in eastern Europe. I imagine that the Americans are not convinced that it is necessary to continue that way whereas many European countries, including (Italy) are much more soft."

He said areas of agreement at the summit were important but were also something of a sweetener to Yeltsin. "He has to sell all these results to his public opinion," Santoro added. "It's just like trying to get someone to accept a bitter pill by coating it with sugar."
